title: I have kept the faith (2 Timothy 4:6–8)
hookLine: Paul near the end: I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course
carry: bring my cloak and the books
tomorrow: Let no man despise thy youth

cards: Tradition says Paul was beheaded outside the walls of Rome, near the road to Ostia, under the emperor Nero.
Pilgrims still visit a great basilica built over the place tradition names as his tomb, Saint Paul Outside the Walls.
In 2009, Pope Benedict the Sixteenth announced that tiny fragments of bone inside the old sarcophagus there had been dated to the first or second century.
Second Timothy presents itself as Paul's last letter, written in chains, knowing what was coming. Today, his farewell.

teach.b: "For I am even now ready to be sacrificed: and the time of my dissolution is at hand." Ready to be sacrificed is one Greek word, spendomai: to be poured out, like wine poured over an altar as an offering.
Paul sees his death that way. Not taken from him. Poured out.
And the Greek word behind dissolution is analysis, a loosening: a ship slipping its moorings, soldiers striking their tents to move on.
Then the sentence people carve on gravestones: "I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith." Three pictures. An athlete or a soldier who stayed in the fight.
A runner who reached the line; remember Paul pressing toward the mark in Philippians. And a guard who kept what was entrusted to him, and handed it on intact.

Then he looks ahead to a crown of justice, which the Lord, the just judge, will give him, and not only him, but all who love his coming. Then, right after the well-known lines, something wonderfully ordinary.

teach.h: BRING MY CLOAK, AND THE BOOKS.
teach.b: Bring my cloak that I left at Troas, he asks Timothy, and the books, especially the parchments. Only Luke is with me. Come before winter.
A man near death, cold, a little lonely, wanting a coat and something to read. The farewell doesn't make him a statue.
Catholics celebrate Paul with Peter every year on June twenty-ninth, the two apostles Rome remembers as martyrs.

Kept the faith doesn't mean a spotless record. Paul never hid that he had once hunted down Christians; he called himself the least of the apostles because of it. It means he didn't put the faith down.

how: Catholics celebrate the Solemnity of Saints Peter and Paul on June 29, and pilgrims to Rome pray at the Basilica of Saint Paul Outside the Walls, built over the place tradition names as his tomb.

games.q: you're Paul in chains, near the end, writing to Timothy. what do you ask for, after your well-known farewell?
o: your cloak, your books, and for Timothy to come before winter.
games.why: "bring my cloak... and the books, especially the parchments." the farewell ends in ordinary human needs.

practice: Think of something you started and left unfinished: a letter, a book, a repair, an apology, a promise to visit.

Choose one you could actually finish, or take one real step on, and picture the finish line, the last page turned, the door knocked on. If you pray, ask for the strength to finish it; if not, simply choose when you'll do it.

wordCard.voice: Spendomai, poured out. Paul's picture of his own death: not taken from him, but poured out like a drink offering. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: I am being poured out, like a drink offering (2 Timothy 4:6; also Philippians 2:17).

carryVoice: Your line: bring my cloak and the books. The great farewell ends with a coat and something to read. That's day five hundred ninety-seven.
